scope: Scene-local provider timing for the retained-message retriever. Revised lines use measured course Kokoro takes. Unchanged beats retain their prior provider words and durations.

changed.previousSay: A customer asks, "Why was my card charged twice?"

beats.say: Why was my card charged twice?
Search these four notes.
Which two mention both words, charged and twice?
M0 and M2 match both.
Start with the support notes in a list of numbered slots. Slot two reaches the plan-change note directly. Its message ID belongs to the note; the slot describes its current position.

Here the illustrative backing array is full. Make a larger array, copy the three references, then append the new note. Spare slots make later appends cheap; occasional copying gives amortized constant work.
Insert a reference at the front and move every existing reference one slot right. Their message IDs stay fixed. This operation takes linear work. Keep the IDs fixed as the query looks them up.

Test the question against the notes. The simplest search opens every note. Lowercase the words and ignore punctuation in this tiny tokenizer. Move down the list, count matching query words, and keep each score with its message ID.
The sign-in note earned no score, but the scan still read it. Repeated questions repeat that work. We can prepare a different direction of lookup before the next request.

A repeated scan reopens every note. Turn that route around: build a dictionary whose keys are words. Read the first note: charged receives its message ID, then twice receives the same ID. We are displaying two entries of the full dictionary.
The sign-in note contributes other words. The plan-change note contains both query words, so add its ID to both collections. Each word now leads back to the notes that supplied it.
The once-charged note adds its ID only to charged. Each value is a set of message IDs. A lookup keeps the original word as its key; hash collisions are resolved by comparing keys.
M0 says, "My card was charged twice. I checked the statement twice." Follow the first occurrence into the twice posting. The set stores its ID; a separate frequency field records one.
Now insert the second occurrence. The same ID is already present, so the set stays unchanged while frequency reaches two. Our binary scorer awards one point for this query word.
Look up charged and visit its posting IDs. Each visited ID adds one to its score counter. A hash lookup takes expected constant work; scoring still visits every ID in the posting.
Look up twice. M0 and M2 now match both words, scoring two each. That's our answer. A score dictionary holds the totals; the heap keeps the top two as candidates arrive.
The posting counters now hold candidate scores. Keep the two strongest notes in a min-heap. Put the once-charged note into the root, the position we inspect when something stronger arrives.
The plan-change note has two points and enters the child slot. The parent is weaker than its child. Only that partial order is required inside the heap.
The earlier note also has two points. The heap is full. Predict which retained note should leave before we move anything.

The weaker root leaves and the earlier note takes its place. Tied scores favor the lower message ID. Restore the heap by moving the plan-change note up and the earlier note down. The root is again the next result to evict.

The posting counters skip M1. Bring back its score from the scan. Zero fails the positive-score check, so we discard M1 without comparing it with the root. M2 keeps its place. Sort the winners strongest first. A bounded heap uses space for two winners, while the score dictionary still holds its candidates.
The corpus keeps growing, so each new support note becomes an indexing job. Claim the oldest waiting job from the left. A deque advances its head while the other references keep their positions.
A list can return the same job, but removing slot zero shifts every remaining reference. A deque makes repeated end operations constant work. Claim order is the first promise to protect.

Two workers claim jobs in arrival order. The second worker can finish first. Keep its result attached to its message ID; the first worker still owns the older job. Then the older job finishes under its own ID.

A separate two-slot ring buffer holds waiting jobs. Its head marks the oldest slot. A new job must wait outside it. After a worker claims the oldest job, admit the pending job into the free slot. No unprocessed job is overwritten.

A separate synchronized queue starts with just M3. Worker B calls get nowait and takes M3. Worker A tries the same call. The queue raises Empty, and A catches it. An earlier nonempty check reserves nothing. This in-memory ordering still needs durable completion and retry handling in a shared service.

If the customer asks for billing notes, a topic tree narrows the same candidate pool. It gives each note one parent. Follow billing and visit its descendants; the access branch stays outside this subtree. A topic tree organizes categories, while a search tree orders keys.

Related notes can have several cross-links. Start with the first note queued and discovered. Follow its neighbors, mark each newly discovered ID, and then enqueue it. The queue stores work; the set prevents duplicate discovery.

One neighbor points to a note already waiting. Another points back to the start. Both IDs are already discovered, so neither enters the queue again. Each reachable note is expanded once in this fixed graph.
Autocomplete asks a different question: which words begin with charg? A trie follows one symbol per edge. Walk the shared prefix once, keeping the suffix branches waiting.

Now continue to the complete word charge and its endings. End markers identify charge, charged and charges. Only charged appears in these four notes. Its posting contains M0, M2 and M3. Reaching a prefix depends on its length. Listing the completions also takes time to visit the branches and return the words.

The search has produced two ranked IDs. Store that result under a key containing the query, result limit and corpus version. A matching request can reuse it. A shared service also separates permission scopes and scoring rules.
A caller borrowing a mutable list can remove its first item and change the next hit. Replay that mutation on a request-owned copy instead. The cached tuple and the next caller keep both original IDs.
Copying fixes ownership. Access needs its own rule. This caller cannot read the first note. Taking two global winners and then removing that note leaves only one accessible result.

Filter the candidate pool by permission before choosing two winners. The once-charged note can now fill the second slot. Share cached results only across compatible permission scopes, or include that scope in the key.
M2 now says, "I can sign in after changing plans." Remove its ID from the postings for was, charged and twice. Add it to can, sign and in. Its other postings stay the same.
Publish the edited notes, index and version together. Return to the original caller, who can read all four notes. Their saved pair, M0 and M2, stays with v7. The v8 lookup misses.
M0 scores two and M3 scores one. For this caller, store their IDs under the v8 query key. An eviction budget limits old versions.
Use the original permission scope. Look up the two words we chose, charged and twice. Charged gives M0 and M3 one point each. Twice gives M0 another point. Send M0 first, then M3.
